h1: Bravo hops for fruity high alpha bittering on a budget
title: Bravo Hops for Fruity High Alpha Bitter | Craft Beer School
desc: How Bravo hops work as a high alpha bittering hop with a fruity edge: the utilisation arithmetic, cost per unit of alpha and storage in Indian heat.
teaser: A bittering hop that also tastes of something. Here is how to dose Bravo and why the price per kilogram misleads.
standfirst: Bravo is a high alpha American hop that brewers use to build bitterness with fewer kilograms in the kettle. It carries a fruity, slightly creamy character that cleaner bittering hops lack. This guide covers the arithmetic, the flavour and the storage.
sections:
Bravo is an American high alpha hop. Grower sheets put its alpha acids at roughly 14 to 17%, though the figure moves with crop year and farm. Alpha acids are the compounds that turn into bitter iso-alpha acids during the boil, so a hop with three times the alpha gives the same bitterness from about a third of the weight.

That is the case for any high alpha hop. Bravo adds a second argument: a fruity, orange-like and faintly creamy character that stays in the beer at the levels a bittering charge uses. Clean bittering hops aim to disappear. Bravo is for brewers who would rather the bitterness had a little flavour of its own, in a pale ale or an IPA where a neutral base would feel flat.

Utilisation is the share of the alpha acid in the kettle that ends up as bitterness in the beer. For a 60 minute boil of normal strength wort with pellets, 25 to 30% is a sensible planning figure. Your own kit and gravity will move it.

The working formula is grams of hop = IBU x litres / (alpha fraction x utilisation x 1,000). For 1,000 L of wort at 37 IBU with Bravo at 15% alpha and 25% utilisation, that is 37 x 1,000 / (0.15 x 0.25 x 1,000), or about 990 g. A 5% alpha hop needs close to 3 kg for the same bitterness.

Those extra kilograms are not free. Pellets soak up wort and carry it into the trub. A heavy bittering charge also adds more vegetal matter for the whirlpool and the fermenter to handle. High alpha hops keep that load small.
Cost per unit of alpha, not per kilogram

A quoted price per kilogram tells you little. The number to compare is the cost of each kilogram of alpha acid. Take the price per kilogram and divide it by the alpha fraction.

As an illustration with made up round numbers: a 5% alpha hop at 100 currency units a kilogram costs 2,000 units per kilogram of alpha. A 15% alpha hop at 150 units a kilogram costs 1,000. The dearer bag is the cheaper bitterness. Freight and cold storage are charged by weight, which tilts the sums further towards high alpha hops, so check the landed cost per kilogram of alpha for your own supplier.

Use the alpha on the certificate of analysis for the crop year you actually buy, not the figure on the label or in a book.
What the flavour does in the beer

Hops added at the start of a 60 minute boil lose most of their essential oils to evaporation. What stays is bitterness and a little background character. Bravo keeps more of that background than most high alpha hops, so a beer bittered with it tastes slightly rounder and fruitier than one bittered with a neutral hop at the same IBU.

If the beer is meant to be dry and crisp, such as a pale lager, that background can read as out of place. If it is a pale ale or IPA with fruity late hops, it tends to blend in. Taste it before you commit a whole brew.
Where it fits in a recipe

Most brewers use Bravo as the first addition and then add aroma hops later. A common plan is Bravo at 60 minutes for most of the IBUs, a small second addition at 10 minutes and a whirlpool stand below about 80 °C with your aroma hops. For the sibling bittering choices, compare Warrior, Herkules and Agnus.

The best test is a split batch. Brew one wort, divide it into two fermenters and bitter one with Bravo and one with your current hop at the same calculated IBU. Taste them side by side at the same temperature. That kind of controlled comparison is the habit our advanced course builds on hop choice.

Alpha acids oxidise over time and the loss speeds up with warmth and air. A pellet bag that has crossed an Indian summer in an unrefrigerated truck can arrive with a lower alpha than the label. Keep vacuum packed pellets in a cold room or freezer, open a bag only as you use it and reseal the rest with the air pressed out.

If you hold hops for months, send a sample for lab alpha analysis or at least keep a record of the supplier's figure and the date. Then adjust the charge. Buying only what a quarter of brewing needs is cheaper than a stale cupboard.
faqs: Is Bravo a bittering hop or an aroma hop?
It is mainly used for bittering because of its high alpha acids, but it carries more fruity character than most hops in that class, so some brewers also use it late.
How much Bravo do I need for 30 IBU?
It depends on volume and utilisation. At 15% alpha and 25% utilisation you need roughly 800 g per 1,000 L of wort. Use the formula in this guide with your own figures.
Can I swap Bravo for another high alpha hop?
Yes, at the same alpha content for the same bitterness. The flavour will change slightly, so taste a test batch before you swap in a recipe you sell.
